name: AI in Radiology Practice
blurb: What prospective studies show about AI in reading images.
title: AI in Radiology Practice
answer: Radiology has the most authorized AI tools, and prospective trials are now testing them in real screening programmes. In one breast screening study, AI supported reading detected cancers with 80.5 percent sensitivity against 73.8 percent for standard double reading, without more interval cancers.

reading.body:
Radiology leads all medical specialties in authorized AI tools, and prospective screening trials now show AI-supported reading outperforming standard double reading.

The pattern is authorization first, evidence second. Radiology accumulated the large majority of AI-enabled devices on the FDA list before prospective trials reported outcomes. The breast screening result is the first clear sign that the evidence base is catching up to the installed base: 80.5 percent sensitivity against 73.8 percent, with interval cancers no worse.

For AI scaling, this matters because radiology is the one clinical domain where the model output is checked against a measurable ground truth and the workflow already runs on digital images. That combination is rare in health care. It is also why radiology is a poor template for other specialties, where the input is text or judgment and the outcome is not a pixel-level label.

The data does not say how many of those authorized devices are actually deployed, what they cost, or whether the sensitivity gain holds outside the single screening programme studied. It also does not cover compute or power, and nothing here supports a claim about either.

The sensitivity comparison is between two reading workflows, not between a human and a machine. Standard double reading means two radiologists read each image, and the AI-supported arm reached 80.5 percent against 73.8 percent for that two-reader baseline. The interval cancer result is what makes the comparison usable, because a screening test that finds more cancers at the moment of reading but misses the same number in the following years has moved detection earlier without changing outcomes. Non-inferior interval cancers means the extra detections held up.

The authorization count and the trial result come from different sources and different years, and the data does not connect them. The FDA list is a count of cleared devices, and the screening study is a single prospective programme. Nothing in the data says the devices on the list include the one used in the study, or that any cleared device has been tested prospectively at all. The gap between the installed base and the evidence base is the actual finding here, and it is a gap in coverage rather than a gap in quality.

The five papers attached to this topic are mostly about integration and practice rather than accuracy. Two are primers and tutorials on using language models in radiology, one is a survey of European Society of Radiology members on practical experience, one is a 2020 recommendations paper on integrating AI into clinical practice, and the oldest is a 2010 piece on decision support. The citation counts run from 324 down to 35, and the two most cited are the two about how to use the tools rather than whether they work. That ordering suggests the field's attention has moved to deployment questions.

What does 80.5 percent sensitivity against 73.8 percent actually mean for a patient?

It means the AI-supported reading found a larger share of the cancers that were present in the screened group than standard double reading did. The data does not give the absolute number of cancers or the size of the screened population, so it cannot be converted into cancers detected per thousand women.

Does the higher sensitivity come with more false positives?

The data does not report false positive rates, recall rates, or biopsy rates for either arm. It reports sensitivity and interval cancers only, so the tradeoff between finding more cancers and flagging more healthy people cannot be assessed from what is here.

How many radiology AI devices are authorized, and how many are in use?

Radiology accounts for the large majority of devices on the FDA's AI-enabled device list, per a 2025 development entry. The data does not give a total count and does not say how many are deployed in clinical practice.

Is the breast screening result enough to justify adopting AI reading elsewhere?

The data covers one prospective screening study in one programme. It does not say whether the sensitivity gain holds in other populations, other equipment, or other screening intervals, and the page's own guidance is to look for prospective evidence in a population like yours before buying.

Do the papers listed test accuracy or something else?

None of the five titles describes a prospective accuracy trial. They cover clinical integration, practical experience, decision support, and how to use large language models in radiology research and deployment.

Does any of this connect to compute or power constraints?

No. The data contains no compute, data center, or electricity figures, and nothing in it supports a claim about either.
